{{Short description|Category theory constructs}}
'''Kan extensions''' are [[Universal property|universal constructs]] in [[category theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]]. They are closely related to [[Adjoint functors|adjoints]], but are also related to [[Limit (category theory)|limits]] and [[End (category theory)|ends]]. They are named after [[Daniel Kan|Daniel M. Kan]], who constructed certain (Kan) extensions using [[Limit (category theory)|limits]] in 1960.

An early use of (what is now known as) a Kan extension from 1956 was in [[homological algebra]] to compute [[derived functor]]s.

In ''[[Categories for the Working Mathematician]]'', [[Saunders Mac Lane]] titled a section "All Concepts Are Kan Extensions", and went on to write that

:The notion of Kan extensions subsumes all the other fundamental concepts of category theory.

Kan extensions generalize the notion of extending a function defined on a subset to a function defined on the whole set. The definition, not surprisingly, is at a high level of abstraction. When specialised to [[poset]]s, it becomes a relatively familiar type of question on [[constrained optimization]].

==Definition==

A Kan extension proceeds from the data of three categories 

:<math>\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{C}</math>

and two [[functor]]s

:<math>X : \mathbf{A} \to \mathbf{C}, F : \mathbf{A} \to \mathbf{B}</math>,

and comes in two varieties: the "left" Kan extension and the "right" Kan extension of <math>X</math> along <math>F</math>.

Abstractly, the functor <math> F</math> gives a pullback map <math> F^* : [\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}] \to [\mathbf{A},\mathbf{C}] </math>. When they exist, the left and right adjoints to <math> F^*</math> applied to <math>X</math> gives the left and right Kan extensions. Spelling the definition of adjoints out, we get the following definitions;

The right Kan extension amounts to finding the dashed functor and the [[natural transformation]] <math>\epsilon</math> in the following diagram:

:<div style="text-align: left;">[[File:RightKanExtension.svg|Right Kan Extension|class=skin-invert]]</div>

Formally, the '''right Kan extension of <math>X</math> along <math>F</math>''' consists of a functor <math>R: \mathbf{B} \to \mathbf{C}</math> and a natural transformation <math>\epsilon: RF \to X</math> that is [[terminal object|terminal]] with respect to this specification, in the sense that for any functor <math>M: \mathbf{B} \to \mathbf{C}</math> and natural transformation <math>\mu: MF \to X</math>, a unique natural transformation <math>\delta: M \to R</math> is defined and fits into a commutative diagram:

:<div style="text-align: left;">[[Image:RightKanExtension universal property.svg|class=skin-invert]]</div> 

where <math>\delta_F</math> is the natural transformation with <math>\delta_F(a) = \delta(Fa): MF(a) \to RF(a)</math> for any [[object (category theory)|object]] <math>a</math> of <math>\mathbf{A}.</math>

The functor ''R'' is often written <math>\operatorname{Ran}_FX</math>.

As with the other [[Universal property|universal constructs]] in [[category theory]], the "left" version of the Kan extension is [[Dual (category theory)|dual]] to the "right" one and is obtained by replacing all categories by their [[opposite category|opposite]]s. 

The effect of this on the description above is merely to reverse the direction of the natural transformations. 

:(Recall that a [[natural transformation]] <math>\tau</math> between the functors <math>F,G: \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}</math> consists of having an [[morphism|arrow]] <math>\tau(a): F(a) \to G(a)</math> for every object <math>a</math> of <math>\mathbf{C}</math>, satisfying a "naturality" property. When we pass to the opposite categories, the source and target of <math>\tau(a)</math> are swapped, causing <math>\tau</math> to act in the opposite direction).

This gives rise to the alternate description: the '''left Kan extension of <math>X</math> along <math>F</math>''' consists of a functor <math>L: \mathbf{B} \to \mathbf{C}</math> and a natural transformation <math>\eta: X \to L F</math> that is [[initial object|initial]] with respect to this specification, in the sense that for any other functor <math>M: \mathbf{B} \to \mathbf{C}</math> and natural transformation <math>\alpha: X \to M F</math>, a unique natural transformation <math>\sigma: L \to M</math> exists and fits into a commutative diagram:

:<div style="text-align: left;">[[File:LeftKanExtension.svg|Left Kan Extension|class=skin-invert]] [[Image:LeftKanExtension universal property.svg|class=skin-invert]]</div>

where <math>\sigma_F</math> is the natural transformation with <math>\sigma_F(a) = \sigma(Fa): LF(a) \to MF(a)</math> for any object <math>a</math> of <math>\mathbf{A}</math>.

The functor ''L'' is often written <math>\operatorname{Lan}_FX</math>.

The use of the word "the" (as in "the left Kan extension") is justified by the fact that, as with all universal constructions, if the object defined exists, then it is unique [[up to]] unique [[isomorphism]]. In this case, that means that (for left Kan extensions) if <math>L, M</math> are two left Kan extensions of <math>X</math> along <math>F</math>, and <math>\eta, \alpha</math> are the corresponding transformations, then there exists a unique ''isomorphism'' of functors <math>\sigma: L \to M</math> such that the second diagram above commutes. Likewise for right Kan extensions.

==Properties==
===Kan extensions as (co)limits===
{{see|limit (category theory)}}
Suppose <math>X:\mathbf{A}\to\mathbf{C}</math> and <math>F:\mathbf{A}\to\mathbf{B}</math> are two functors. If '''A''' is [[small category|small]] and '''C''' is cocomplete, then there exists a left Kan extension <math>\operatorname{Lan}_FX</math> of <math>X</math> along <math>F</math>, defined at each object ''b'' of '''B''' by

:<math>(\operatorname{Lan}_F X)(b) = \varinjlim_{f:Fa \to b} X(a)</math>

where the colimit is taken over the [[comma category]] <math>(F \downarrow \operatorname{const}_b)</math>, where <math>\operatorname{const}_b\colon \ast\to \mathbf{B}, \ast\mapsto b</math> is the constant functor. Dually, if '''A''' is small and '''C''' is complete, then right Kan extensions along <math>F</math> exist, and can be computed as the limit 

:<math>(\operatorname{Ran}_F X)(b) = \varprojlim_{Fa \leftarrow b} X(a)</math>

over the comma category <math>(\operatorname{const}_b \downarrow F)</math>.

===Kan extensions as (co)ends===
{{see|coend (category theory)}}
Suppose <math>X:\mathbf{A}\to\mathbf{C}</math> and <math>F:\mathbf{A}\to\mathbf{B}</math> are two functors such that for all objects ''a'' and ''a{{prime}}'' of '''A''' and all objects ''b'' of '''B''', the [[copower (category theory)|copowers]] <math>\mathbf{B}(Fa',b)\cdot Xa</math> exist in '''C'''. Then the functor ''X'' has a left Kan extension <math>\operatorname{Lan}_FX</math> along ''F'', which is such that, for every object ''b'' of '''B''',

:<math>(\operatorname{Lan}_FX)b=\int^a \mathbf{B}(Fa,b)\cdot Xa</math>

when the above [[coend (category theory)|coend]] exists for every object ''b'' of '''B'''.

Dually, right Kan extensions can be computed by the [[end (category theory)|end]] formula

:<math>(\operatorname{Ran}_FX)b=\int_a Xa^{\mathbf{B}(b,Fa)}.</math>

===Limits as Kan extensions===
The [[Limit (category theory)|limit]] of a functor <math>F: \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}</math> can be expressed as a Kan extension by

:<math>\lim F = \operatorname{Ran}_E F</math>

where <math>E</math> is the unique functor from <math>\mathbf{C}</math> to <math>\mathbf{1}</math> (the [[category (mathematics)|category]] with one object and one arrow, a [[terminal object]] in <math>\mathbf{Cat}</math>). The colimit of <math>F</math> can be expressed similarly by

:<math>\operatorname{colim} F = \operatorname{Lan}_E F.</math>

===Adjoints as Kan extensions===
A functor <math>F : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}</math> possesses a [[left adjoint]] [[if and only if]] the right Kan extension of <math>\operatorname{Id} : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{C}</math> along <math>F</math> exists and is preserved by <math>F</math>. In this case, a left adjoint is given by <math>\operatorname{Ran}_F \operatorname{Id}</math> and this Kan extension is even preserved by any functor <math>\mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{E}</math> whatsoever, i.e. is an ''absolute'' Kan extension.

Dually, a right adjoint exists if and only if the left Kan extension of the identity along <math>F</math> exists and is preserved by <math>F</math>.

==Applications==

The [[codensity monad]] of a functor <math>G: \mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{C}</math> is a right Kan extension of ''G'' along itself.
